title: Supersonic Passenger Flight Stalled for Fifty Years — the Engine, Not Aerodynamics, Was the Blocker
dek: Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because the sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and that engine is now going to data centers to generate power first.
why: A founder's first-person account of the full path from being turned down by Bezos to building his own engine and pivoting into data-center power generation, with specific numbers and regulatory detail, high information density.
who: Founders and investors watching hard-tech startups, aviation and data-center energy — especially anyone who wants to see how a hardware company uses another market to feed its main business.
skip: The opening 0:00-4:10 is launch-event-style setup and a promo video; skip to 5:12 for the actual discussion.

points.h: Bend the sonic boom and the ban disappears
points.body: Boom's solution to the sonic boom is not to make the aircraft quiet, but to use the atmosphere's own refractive capacity to redirect the boom back up into the sky. Blake calls this boomless cruise; engineers call it Mach cutoff: the boom is still generated at the aircraft as usual, at normal strength, but it bends sharply in the air and never reaches the ground. This works below Mach 1.3 — that is, 50% faster than today. So you can't go full speed over land, but a 9 a.m. departure from New York landing in San Francisco at 9:30 still holds. Over the ocean no one is listening, so full speed is fine. Push the logic to its limit and you get the line: if there's no sonic boom at all, there's nothing to argue about.

points.h: From executive order to act of Congress, unanimous
points.body: The U.S. ban on supersonic flight over land, in place since 1973, ended on June 6 last year. But Blake knew an executive order can in theory be overturned by the next person, so he turned to pushing Congress. The Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House unanimously and recently cleared a Senate committee unanimously as well. He put the significance plainly: supersonic isn't a partisan issue, which is the only way to get that kind of vote. For a hardware company that has to span multiple administrations on a timeline measured in decades, upgrading regulation from executive order to law turns policy risk from a variable into a constant.

points.h: Getting stood up by a big company saved the company
points.body: Blake says one of the dumbest things he ever did was outsource engine development to an established large company; the plan failed, Boom split publicly with Rolls-Royce, and everyone said Boom was finished. So they decided to do what everyone said was impossible: build the engine from scratch, and not just design it — even the hardest parts, like turbine blades, they make themselves. His judgment: engineering and manufacturing have to be done together, and if you want to reindustrialize America you have to invent the next generation of manufacturing technology here, not bring back what was offshored to China. That forced choice later became the source of the company's valuation — because an engine designed to run at high temperature, full power, for long durations at Mach 1.7, once you take off the front fan and bolt a generator on the back, is a power generation device.

points.h: The supersonic engine's first customer is a data center
points.body: Boom's engine's first application isn't in the sky, it's on the ground. Take off the fan, swap in a generator at the back, put it in a few trailers, and you can do 42 megawatts of behind-the-meter generation — and because the engine core was designed to run at high temperature, it needs no water. Blake specifically calls out that water is a common objection, so just make it disappear. The factory has already started producing the first parts, the target is multiple gigawatts a year, and more than 10 gigawatts added to the grid over the next five years. The financial significance of this path: before the supersonic airliner gets its airworthiness certificate, the company already has a product it can sell — and it's selling to the buyer who currently has the most money.

points.h: Run on the ground first, then fly
points.body: Boom putting the engine to work in ground power generation first has an engineering side effect: it will be the most-tested new jet engine in history, because it will have run for enormous numbers of hours on the ground before ever being installed and flown. Blake admits many hard problems remain and success isn't guaranteed. The promise to passengers: twice as fast over the ocean, 50% faster over land with no sonic boom. The sequencing itself is worth noting — normally an aviation engine's validation comes from accumulating flight hours, and Boom has moved validation to the ground and to data-center scenarios, effectively having another market pay the test costs for the aviation business.

The numbers Blake gives: a Mach 1.7 transatlantic round trip in 3 hours, breakeven fare around $3,500, actual ticket price probably higher, and every extra dollar is United's profit. His assessment of Concorde: zero out of three on safe, comfortable and cheap; Boom wants all three. On timeline, the target is 4 years, but he says explicitly that ‘fast matters more than predictable’, can't give a firm date, and only promises to deliver at the earliest time physically possible — from the outside that looks like around 2030. There's a tradeoff worth noting here: a hardware company publicly admitting it's unpredictable, trading certainty for speed.

points.h: Data-center demand is so large they'll auction it
points.body: Asked whether the data-center business is a money printer, Blake's answer is ‘it's the most incredible money-printing business I've ever seen’, and says there are tens of gigawatts of demand in his inbox. The first engine fires up next month, and then they plan to auction off all the capacity. Asked whether he's talked to Elon, whether it's for Colossus, Blake only says ‘you should ask Elon’. The value of this segment is that it gives an anomalous supply-demand signal: for a power product that isn't in mass production yet, demand already far exceeds capacity, and the pricing mechanism has shifted from a quote to an auction.

points.h: Break the sound barrier Monday, model in the Oval Office Thursday
points.body: Blake recaps the speed of this regulatory push: Monday, break the sound barrier, post it, Elon reposts, fly to Washington that night to start the legalization lobbying, and by the time he lands there's already a White House invitation; Tuesday, into the West Wing; Thursday, the aircraft model goes into the Oval Office — and it's still there. From launch to signature, the executive order took 115 days, which he thinks is slow, though he admits another administration would be slower. His assessment of this administration: ‘I like that it moves fast’. This is the most concrete policy-operations sample in the whole episode: how a technical milestone gets converted directly into political attention.
